title: Fruits lowest in sugar

seo.title: Fruits lowest in sugar
seo.meta_description: Per 100 g, avocado has ~0.7 g sugar; lime 1.7; lemon 2.5; raspberries 4.4; blackberries 4.9; strawberries 4.9; watermelon 6.2 and grapefruit 6.9 g. Serving size still matters.
seo.search_intent: Rank common fresh fruits with the lowest total sugar per 100 g and explain why lower sugar does not necessarily mean lower calories.

excerpt: Among common fresh fruits, avocado is an outlier at only about 0.7 g total sugar per 100 g. Other low-sugar examples include lime (~1.7 g), lemon (~2.5 g), raspberries (4.4 g), blackberries (4.9 g), strawberries (4.9 g), watermelon (6.2 g) and pink/red grapefruit (6.9 g). Per-100-g rankings compare concentration; serving size and total nutrition still matter.
content_html:
Fruit does not come with one fixed amount of sugar. An avocado, a bowl of raspberries and a banana are all fruit, but their macronutrient profiles are very different. To compare concentration fairly, the useful starting point is total sugars per 100 g of raw edible fruit.

Low-sugar fresh fruit ranking

Ripeness can shift the numbers within the same fruit. As some fruits mature, their carbohydrate profile changes and perceived sweetness increases, while variety also matters. A ranking is therefore a useful approximation rather than a promise that every individual piece contains exactly the same amount. In everyday eating, choosing a reasonable serving of a fruit you enjoy usually matters more than trying to separate two similar options by a fraction of a gram of sugar.

These are USDA reference values for raw fruit. Juice, dried fruit and products with added sugar are not equivalent comparisons.

FruitSugars per 100 gCalories per 100 g
Avocado0.7 g160 kcal
Lime1.7 g30 kcal
Lemon2.5 g29 kcal
Raspberries4.4 g52 kcal
Blackberries4.9 g43 kcal
Strawberries4.9 g32 kcal
Watermelon6.2 g30 kcal
Pink/red grapefruit6.9 g42 kcal

Two different patterns appear. Tart citrus fruits are very low in sugar, although lemon and lime are rarely eaten in large stand-alone servings. Berries sit around 4–5 g sugar per 100 g while also providing meaningful fiber.

Avocado is lowest in sugar, not calories

Whole fruit behaves differently from juice or a heavily strained puree. The food structure, fiber, and speed of consumption change the experience of fullness. A whole fruit with somewhat more total sugar may be a more useful choice than a low-volume drink that is consumed in seconds. If the goal is to moderate sugar intake, favoring intact fruit and paying attention to portion size often has more practical impact than chasing the very lowest position on a ranking.

Avocado contains only about 0.66 g sugar per 100 g, but around 160 calories because it contains nearly 15 g fat. Watermelon has 6.2 g sugar yet only 30 calories per 100 g.

That is why “lower sugar” and “lower calorie” are not interchangeable goals.

Berries combine low sugar with fiber

Raspberries, blackberries and strawberries cluster around 4.4–4.9 g sugar per 100 g. Raspberries also provide about 6.5 g fiber/100 g, while blackberries provide roughly 5.3 g.

Strawberries contain less fiber than those two but are especially low in energy at about 32 calories per 100 g.

Serving size changes the amount you actually eat

Sugar should also be separated from energy density. Avocado and olives are botanical fruits with very little sugar, yet they contain more fat and calories than many sweet fruits. That does not make them worse foods; it simply shows that 'lower sugar' does not automatically mean 'lower calorie.' In the other direction, a fruit with more sugar can still contain a great deal of water and have a relatively low energy density. The useful metric depends on the goal.

A 150 g serving of strawberries contains about 7.3 g sugar. A generous 250 g serving of watermelon contains around 15.5 g. Watermelon remains relatively low in sugar by weight, but a much larger serving naturally contributes more total grams.

Do you need to choose only the lowest-sugar fruit?

For diabetes or eating plans with specific carbohydrate targets, total serving size and the rest of the meal may matter more than a general fruit ranking. Pairing fruit with yogurt, nuts, or another source of protein or fat changes the meal context. Individual needs and medication can also affect the strategy. For the general population, rotating different whole fruits and not treating their natural sugar as a reason to avoid them is usually a more balanced way to use the information.

Usually not. Whole fruit comes packaged with water, fiber, vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals, and its naturally occurring sugar is part of that food matrix.

The ranking is useful when sugar concentration is the specific question. For everyday choices, fiber, calories, serving size, variety and what you actually enjoy eating also matter.

faq.question: What fruit has the least sugar?
faq.answer: Among common fresh fruits, avocado is exceptionally low at about 0.7 g per 100 g, although it is much higher in calories than watery fruit.

faq.question: Which berries are lowest in sugar?
faq.answer: Raspberries, blackberries and strawberries are all around 4.4–4.9 g total sugar per 100 g.

faq.question: Is watermelon high in sugar?
faq.answer: By weight it is relatively low at about 6.2 g per 100 g, but a large serving contains more total grams.
